title: "Impact-calibrated infit bands, validation"
subtitle: "Upper side of the band from second-dimension misfit, against a same-item counterfactual"
author: "Magnus Johansson"
date: today
---

```{r setup}
#| include: false
suppressMessages({
  library(dplyr)
  library(tidyr)
  library(knitr)
  library(ggplot2)
})
fs <- list.files("infit_impact_validation", pattern = "_rho[0-9]{3}(_n[0-9]{5})?[.]rds$",
                 full.names = TRUE)
L <- lapply(fs, readRDS)
S_all <- bind_rows(lapply(L, `[[`, "summary")) |>
  mutate(target = factor(target, levels = c("on", "mid", "off")))
S <- S_all |> filter(n == 20000)
minutes <- sum(vapply(L, `[[`, numeric(1), "minutes"))
failed <- sum(vapply(L, function(x) length(x$failed), integer(1)))

# Metric F from the pooled conditional-bias sums: largest absolute difference
# in conditional bias between (a) and (b), in units of the mean SEM at that
# theta, over theta values with at least 200 persons.
Ftab <- bind_rows(lapply(L, function(x) {
  f <- x$fsum
  f <- f[f$n >= 200, ]
  d <- (f$bias_a - f$bias_b) / f$n
  sem <- f$sem_b / f$n
  j <- which.max(abs(d) / sem)
  data.frame(design = x$base_info$design, target = x$base_info$target,
             n = x$base_info$n, rho = x$summary$rho[1], F_sem = abs(d[j]) / sem[j],
             F_logit = abs(d[j]), F_theta = f$theta[j])
})) |>
  mutate(target = factor(target, levels = c("on", "mid", "off")))

cell_all <- S_all |>
  group_by(design, target, item, rel_loc, n, rho) |>
  summarise(msq = mean(msq), other_min = mean(other_msq_min),
            other_max = mean(other_msq_max),
            A_rmse_ratio = mean(rmse_a / rmse_b),
            keep_vs_remove = mean(rmse_a / rmse_c),
            B_shift = mean(shift_mean), B_gt1 = mean(shift_gt1),
            C_kl = mean(kl_mean), C_kl_shift_share = mean(kl_shift) / mean(kl_mean),
            E_wle = mean(E_wle), E_sum = mean(E_sum),
            spear_wle_a = mean(spear_a), spear_sum_a = mean(spear_sum_a),
            reps = n(), .groups = "drop") |>
  left_join(Ftab, by = c("design", "target", "n", "rho"))
cell <- cell_all |> filter(n == 20000)
kb <- function(x, ...) kable(x, ...)
```

## Purpose

An effect-size floor judges an item's infit by an FWB interval for its
population MSQ against a band $[1 - \delta_i^-, 1 + \delta_i^+]$. This study
calibrates the upper side, $\delta_i^+$, from the consequences of misfit for
person scores, and checks that the calibration behaves. The design and the
decisions behind it are in `infit-impact-delta-design.md`. The simulation is
`infit_impact_validation.R`.

## Design

- **Counterfactual.** For a target item $i$ and correlation $\rho$, datasets
  (a) item $i$ responds to $\theta_2$, (b) item $i$ responds to $\theta_1$,
  and (c) item $i$ removed share every person and every uniform draw. Impact
  of the misfit is (a) against (b), both judged against the true
  $\theta_1$. (a) against (c) is the keep-or-remove comparison.
- **Group pair.** A random half of the sample is shifted by 0.5 SD on the
  item-specific factor of $\theta_2$, with $\theta_1$ unchanged, for metric E.
- **Analysis.** CML refit, WLE with SEM, linked to the generating scale
  through the items other than $i$. Sum scores alongside.
- **Designs.** `d20`: 20 dichotomous items evenly spaced on [-2, 2] (the
  Part A design), targets at about 0, -1 and -2 logits from the person mean.
  `phq9`: the package data, 9 items with 4 categories, targets nearest the
  person mean, at the median distance, and farthest away.
- **Persons.** Resampled WLE from a base dataset (2,000 respondents for d20,
  the complete phq9 cases), as in the `dgp = "resample"` cutoffs.
- **Grid.** $\rho$ = .3, .5, .6, .7, .8, .85, .9, .95 and 1. $\rho = 1$ is
  the fitting item, where every impact must be zero.
- **Size.** n = 20,000 per dataset as a population proxy, 40 replicates per
  cell. For the on-target items only, also n = 2,000 and 5,000, to check
  whether the impact estimates move with n. All tables except the stability
  section use n = 20,000.

**Impact metrics** (section 5 of the design note):

| | Metric | Units |
|---|---|---|
| A | RMSE of $\hat\theta - \theta_1$, (a) over (b) | ratio |
| B | mean $|\hat\theta_a - \hat\theta_b| / \text{SEM}_b$, and the share above 1 | SEM |
| C | mean KL between $N(\hat\theta_a, \text{SEM}_a^2)$ and $N(\hat\theta_b, \text{SEM}_b^2)$ | nats |
| E | spurious group difference per SD of group difference on the item-specific factor | SD of $\theta_1$ (WLE) or of the sum score |
| F | largest difference in conditional bias $E(\hat\theta - \theta_1 \mid \theta_1)$ between (a) and (b) | SEM at that $\theta_1$ |

## Checks

```{r checks}
S |>
  group_by(design, target) |>
  summarise(cells = n_distinct(rho), reps = n(),
            impact_at_rho1 = max(abs(c(rmse_a[rho == 1] - rmse_b[rho == 1],
                                       shift_mean[rho == 1], kl_mean[rho == 1],
                                       E_wle[rho == 1]))),
            msq_at_rho1 = mean(msq[rho == 1]), .groups = "drop") |>
  kb(digits = 4)
```

`r failed` replicates failed. About `r round(minutes)` minutes on 10 cores.
At $\rho = 1$ every impact must be exactly 0 and the MSQ near 1.

## MSQ and impact by $\rho$

```{r msq-impact}
cell |>
  select(design, target, rho, msq, other_min, other_max, A_rmse_ratio, B_shift,
         B_gt1, C_kl, E_wle, E_sum, F_sem) |>
  arrange(design, target, desc(rho)) |>
  kb(digits = c(0, 0, 2, 3, 3, 3, 3, 3, 3, 4, 3, 3, 3))
```

`other_min` and `other_max` are the lowest and highest MSQ among the other
items in dataset (a): the cascade caused by one misfitting item.

```{r impact-fig, fig.height = 7}
cell |>
  select(design, target, msq, A_rmse_ratio, B_shift, C_kl, E_wle, F_sem) |>
  mutate(A_rmse_ratio = A_rmse_ratio - 1) |>
  pivot_longer(c(A_rmse_ratio, B_shift, C_kl, E_wle, F_sem),
               names_to = "metric") |>
  ggplot(aes(msq, value, colour = target, linetype = design)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point(size = 1.2) +
  facet_wrap(~ metric, scales = "free_y", ncol = 2) +
  labs(x = "Population MSQ of the misfitting item", y = "Impact",
       colour = "Target", linetype = "Design") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

A for this figure is the RMSE ratio minus 1.

**Monotonicity.** The calibration inverts impact as a function of MSQ, which
needs impact to rise as MSQ rises. Rank correlation over the grid, per item
and metric (1 means perfectly monotone):

```{r monotone}
cell |>
  group_by(design, target) |>
  summarise(across(c(A_rmse_ratio, B_shift, C_kl, E_wle, F_sem),
                   \(v) cor(msq, v, method = "spearman")),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  kb(digits = 2)
```

## Calibrated $\delta^+$

For each item and metric, the MSQ at which impact reaches the tolerance,
read by linear interpolation along the grid, minus 1. `>` means the tolerance
was not reached within the grid (the largest MSQ reached is shown). The
tolerances are illustrations of what a user might choose.

```{r delta}
tol <- tribble(
  ~metric,        ~tau,  ~label,
  "A_rmse_ratio", 1.025, "A: RMSE +2.5%",
  "A_rmse_ratio", 1.05,  "A: RMSE +5%",
  "B_shift",      0.25,  "B: mean shift 0.25 SEM",
  "B_gt1",        0.05,  "B: 5% move > 1 SEM",
  "C_kl",         0.03,  "C: KL 0.03",
  "E_wle",        0.05,  "E: 0.05 SD per SD",
  "E_wle",        0.10,  "E: 0.10 SD per SD",
  "F_sem",        0.25,  "F: 0.25 SEM"
)
invert <- function(msq, v, tau) {
  o <- order(msq); msq <- msq[o]; v <- v[o]
  j <- which(v >= tau)[1]
  if (is.na(j)) return(sprintf(">%.2f", max(msq) - 1))
  if (j == 1) return(sprintf("%.2f", msq[1] - 1))
  x <- msq[j - 1] + (tau - v[j - 1]) * (msq[j] - msq[j - 1]) / (v[j] - v[j - 1])
  sprintf("%.2f", x - 1)
}
cell |>
  group_by(design, target, rel_loc) |>
  group_modify(function(d, key) {
    tibble(label = tol$label,
           delta = mapply(function(m, t) invert(d$msq, d[[m]], t),
                          tol$metric, tol$tau))
  }) |>
  ungroup() |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = label, values_from = delta) |>
  kb(digits = 2)
```

## Keep or remove

RMSE with the misfitting item kept, over RMSE with it removed (dataset c).
Below 1, keeping the item measures $\theta_1$ better despite the misfit. The
table shows the ratio by $\rho$ and the MSQ at which it crosses 1.

```{r keep-remove}
cell |>
  select(design, target, rho, msq, keep_vs_remove) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = rho, values_from = c(msq, keep_vs_remove),
              names_glue = "{.value}_{rho}") |>
  select(design, target, starts_with("keep_vs_remove")) |>
  kb(digits = 3)

cell |>
  group_by(design, target) |>
  summarise(msq_where_equal = {
    o <- order(msq); m <- msq[o]; k <- keep_vs_remove[o]
    j <- which(k >= 1)[1]
    if (is.na(j)) NA_real_ else if (j == 1) m[1] else
      m[j - 1] + (1 - k[j - 1]) * (m[j] - m[j - 1]) / (k[j] - k[j - 1])
  }, .groups = "drop") |>
  kb(digits = 3)
```

## Sum score

With complete data the WLE is a monotone function of the sum score, so their
rank correlations with $\theta_1$ should agree. Metric E differs between the
two because the WLE stretches the scale at the extremes.

```{r sumscore}
cell |>
  filter(rho %in% c(0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9)) |>
  select(design, target, rho, spear_wle_a, spear_sum_a, E_wle, E_sum) |>
  kb(digits = 4)
```

## Stability in n

On-target items only. If an impact metric is estimated without bias, its
mean at n = 2,000 and 5,000 matches n = 20,000. The squared and absolute
metrics (B, C, F) could be biased upward at small n by estimation noise that
does not cancel between datasets (a) and (b).

```{r stability}
cell_all |>
  filter(target == "on", rho %in% c(0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.85, 0.95, 1)) |>
  select(design, rho, n, msq, A_rmse_ratio, B_shift, B_gt1, C_kl, E_wle,
         F_sem) |>
  arrange(design, desc(rho), n) |>
  kb(digits = c(0, 2, 0, 3, 3, 3, 3, 4, 3, 3))
```

## Overfit arm: the lower side, $\delta^-$

Added 2026-10-12. Item $i$ responds to $\theta_1$ with discrimination
$a \geq 1$ (GPCM) at the same location, against the same item with $a = 1$.
Grid: $a$ = 1, 1.15, 1.3, 1.5, 1.75, 2, 2.5 and 3. Same designs, targets,
n = 20,000 and 40 replicates. Metric E is not defined, since there is no
second dimension. Metric D, the true error SD over the reported SEM, is added
for this arm only: overfit is classically said to make reported precision
wrong, and the other metrics cannot show that. D is shown as the ratio of
(a) to (b), so 1 means the steep item does not change how honest the
reported SEM is.

```{r slope-load}
fs_s <- list.files("infit_impact_validation", pattern = "_slope[0-9]{3}[.]rds$",
                   full.names = TRUE)
Ls <- lapply(fs_s, readRDS)
Ss <- bind_rows(lapply(Ls, `[[`, "summary")) |>
  mutate(target = factor(target, levels = c("on", "mid", "off")))
Fs <- bind_rows(lapply(Ls, function(x) {
  f <- x$fsum; f <- f[f$n >= 200, ]
  d <- (f$bias_a - f$bias_b) / f$n; sem <- f$sem_b / f$n
  j <- which.max(abs(d) / sem)
  data.frame(design = x$base_info$design, target = x$base_info$target,
             slope = x$summary$rho[1], F_sem = abs(d[j]) / sem[j],
             F_theta = f$theta[j])
})) |>
  mutate(target = factor(target, levels = c("on", "mid", "off")))
cell_s <- Ss |>
  rename(slope = rho) |>
  group_by(design, target, rel_loc, slope) |>
  summarise(msq = mean(msq), other_min = mean(other_msq_min),
            other_max = mean(other_msq_max),
            A_rmse_ratio = mean(rmse_a / rmse_b),
            keep_vs_remove = mean(rmse_a / rmse_c),
            B_shift = mean(shift_mean), B_gt1 = mean(shift_gt1),
            C_kl = mean(kl_mean), D_ratio = mean(D_a / D_b), D_b = mean(D_b),
            reps = n(), .groups = "drop") |>
  left_join(Fs, by = c("design", "target", "slope"))
```

`r sum(vapply(Ls, function(x) length(x$failed), integer(1)))` replicates
failed.

```{r slope-table}
cell_s |>
  select(design, target, slope, msq, other_min, other_max, A_rmse_ratio,
         B_shift, B_gt1, C_kl, D_ratio, F_sem, keep_vs_remove) |>
  arrange(design, target, slope) |>
  kb(digits = c(0, 0, 2, 3, 3, 3, 3, 3, 4, 4, 3, 3, 3))
```

`other_min` and `other_max` show the cascade from one steep item, which now
pushes the other items toward *underfit*.

**Calibrated $\delta^-$.** The departure $1 - \text{MSQ}$ at which impact
reaches the tolerance, read along the grid. `>` means not reached.

```{r delta-minus}
tol_s <- tol |> filter(!grepl("^E", label))
invert_low <- function(msq, v, tau) {
  dev <- 1 - msq
  o <- order(dev); dev <- dev[o]; v <- v[o]
  j <- which(v >= tau)[1]
  if (is.na(j)) return(sprintf(">%.2f", max(dev)))
  if (j == 1) return(sprintf("%.2f", dev[1]))
  x <- dev[j - 1] + (tau - v[j - 1]) * (dev[j] - dev[j - 1]) / (v[j] - v[j - 1])
  sprintf("%.2f", x)
}
cell_s |>
  group_by(design, target, rel_loc) |>
  group_modify(function(d, key) {
    tibble(label = tol_s$label,
           delta = mapply(function(m, t) invert_low(d$msq, d[[m]], t),
                          tol_s$metric, tol_s$tau))
  }) |>
  ungroup() |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = label, values_from = delta) |>
  kb(digits = 2)
```

## Joint arm: three misfitting items

Added 2026-10-12. The three target items respond to one shared $\theta_2$
with correlation $\rho$, as in Part A. The counterfactual has all three
fitting, and dataset (c) removes all three. The question is how much larger
the joint impact is than the impact of each item alone, which decides how
lenient per-item bands are when several items misfit.

```{r joint-load}
load_mech <- function(pattern) {
  fl <- list.files("infit_impact_validation", pattern = pattern, full.names = TRUE)
  lst <- lapply(fl, readRDS)
  list(L = lst, S = bind_rows(lapply(lst, `[[`, "summary")),
       F = bind_rows(lapply(lst, function(x) {
         f <- x$fsum; f <- f[f$n >= 200, ]
         d <- (f$bias_a - f$bias_b) / f$n; sem <- f$sem_b / f$n
         j <- which.max(abs(d) / sem)
         data.frame(design = x$base_info$design, target = x$base_info$target,
                    par = x$summary$rho[1], F_sem = abs(d[j]) / sem[j])
       })))
}
J <- load_mech("_jointrho[0-9]{3}[.]rds$")
cell_j <- J$S |>
  rename(par = rho) |>
  group_by(design, par) |>
  summarise(msq_1 = mean(msq_1), msq_2 = mean(msq_2), msq_3 = mean(msq_3),
            other_min = mean(other_msq_min), other_max = mean(other_msq_max),
            A_rmse_ratio = mean(rmse_a / rmse_b),
            keep_vs_remove = mean(rmse_a / rmse_c),
            B_shift = mean(shift_mean), C_kl = mean(kl_mean),
            E_wle = mean(E_wle), D_ratio = mean(D_a / D_b), .groups = "drop") |>
  left_join(J$F |> select(design, par, F_sem), by = c("design", "par"))
cell_j |>
  arrange(design, desc(par)) |>
  kb(digits = c(0, 2, 3, 3, 3, 3, 3, 3, 3, 3, 4, 3, 3, 3))
```

`r sum(vapply(J$L, function(x) length(x$failed), integer(1)))` replicates
failed. `msq_1` to `msq_3` are the on, mid and off target items (for d20, the
items near 0, -1 and -2 logits).

**Joint against single.** For each $\rho$, the joint impact next to the sum
of the three single-item impacts from the main arm. A ratio above 1 means the
items do more harm together than separately.

```{r joint-vs-single}
single_sum <- cell |>
  group_by(design, rho) |>
  summarise(A_single_sum = sum(A_rmse_ratio - 1), C_single_sum = sum(C_kl),
            E_single_sum = sum(E_wle), F_single_max = max(F_sem),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  rename(par = rho)
cell_j |>
  left_join(single_sum, by = c("design", "par")) |>
  filter(par < 1) |>
  transmute(design, rho = par, A_joint = A_rmse_ratio - 1, A_single_sum,
            C_joint = C_kl, C_single_sum, C_ratio = C_kl / C_single_sum,
            E_joint = E_wle, E_single_sum, F_joint = F_sem, F_single_max) |>
  arrange(design, desc(rho)) |>
  kb(digits = c(0, 2, 4, 4, 4, 4, 2, 3, 3, 3, 3))
```

**Joint band.** The mean MSQ of the three items at which the joint impact
reaches the tolerance, minus 1.

```{r joint-delta}
cell_j |>
  mutate(msq = (msq_1 + msq_2 + msq_3) / 3) |>
  group_by(design) |>
  group_modify(function(d, key) {
    tibble(label = tol$label,
           delta = mapply(function(m, t) invert(d$msq, d[[m]], t),
                          tol$metric, tol$tau))
  }) |>
  ungroup() |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = label, values_from = delta) |>
  kb()
```

## Local dependence arm: response dependence

Added 2026-10-12. Uniform response dependence as in the log-linear Rasch
model: item $j$, the item nearest the target item $i$ in location, responds
to $\theta_1 + \lambda x_i$, so a higher score on item $i$ makes item $j$
easier. The counterfactual is the same pair without dependence ($\lambda =
0$), and dataset (c) removes item $j$. Grid: $\lambda$ = 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75,
1, 1.5 and 2. Metric E is not defined. Metric D (true error over reported
SEM) is included, since this is where reported precision may become too
optimistic.

```{r ld-table}
D_ld <- load_mech("_ldlambda[0-9]{3}[.]rds$")
cell_ld <- D_ld$S |>
  rename(par = rho) |>
  mutate(target = factor(target, levels = c("on", "mid", "off"))) |>
  group_by(design, target, item, ld_partner, par) |>
  summarise(msq_j = mean(msq), msq_i = mean(msq_partner),
            other_min = mean(other_msq_min), other_max = mean(other_msq_max),
            A_rmse_ratio = mean(rmse_a / rmse_b),
            keep_vs_remove = mean(rmse_a / rmse_c),
            B_shift = mean(shift_mean), B_gt1 = mean(shift_gt1),
            C_kl = mean(kl_mean), D_ratio = mean(D_a / D_b), .groups = "drop") |>
  left_join(D_ld$F |> mutate(target = factor(target, levels = c("on", "mid", "off"))) |>
              select(design, target, par, F_sem),
            by = c("design", "target", "par"))
cell_ld |>
  rename(lambda = par) |>
  arrange(design, target, lambda) |>
  kb(digits = c(0, 0, 0, 0, 2, 3, 3, 3, 3, 3, 3, 3, 4, 4, 3, 3))
```

`r sum(vapply(D_ld$L, function(x) length(x$failed), integer(1)))` replicates
failed. `item` is the target $i$ and `ld_partner` the dependent item $j$.
`msq_j` is the dependent item's MSQ and `msq_i` the target's. A `D_ratio`
below 1 means the reported SEM understates the true error once the
dependence is present.

**Calibrated $\delta^-$ from response dependence**, on the dependent item's
MSQ, as $1 - \text{MSQ}$.

```{r ld-delta}
tol_ld <- bind_rows(tol |> filter(!grepl("^E", label)),
                    tibble(metric = "D_gap", tau = 0.05,
                           label = "D: SEM 5% too optimistic"))
cell_ld |>
  mutate(D_gap = 1 - D_ratio) |>
  group_by(design, target) |>
  group_modify(function(d, key) {
    tibble(label = tol_ld$label,
           delta = mapply(function(m, t) invert_low(d$msq_j, d[[m]], t),
                          tol_ld$metric, tol_ld$tau))
  }) |>
  ungroup() |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = label, values_from = delta) |>
  kb()
```

## Impact intervals

The floor turns a tolerance into a band and asks whether an item's MSQ
interval lies inside it. The reverse is also possible: map the item's FWB
interval for its MSQ through the impact curve, giving an interval for the
item's *impact* in the metric's own units. No tolerance is needed to report
it, and the user can judge the consequence directly.

The impact curve for an item combines the overfit arm (MSQ below 1, slope
mechanism) and the main arm (MSQ above 1, second dimension), with impact 0 at
MSQ = 1. Because impact is smallest at 1, an MSQ interval that contains 1
maps to an impact interval starting at 0. Otherwise the endpoints map to the
endpoints.

The demonstration uses the FWB intervals from `fwb_msq_coverage.qmd`
(d20 design, normal persons), mapped through the d20 curves calibrated here
(resampled WLE persons, base SD 1.58 against 1.5, so the curves are close
but not identical). The items are the one misfitting item at 0 logits
($\rho = .50$, population MSQ 1.38) and, for contrast, a fitting item under
the null.

```{r impact-intervals}
curve_for <- function(dsg, tgt, metric) {
  up <- cell |> filter(design == dsg, target == tgt) |>
    select(msq, v = all_of(metric))
  lo <- cell_s |> filter(design == dsg, target == tgt) |>
    select(msq, v = all_of(metric))
  bind_rows(lo, up, tibble(msq = 1, v = 0)) |>
    group_by(msq) |> summarise(v = mean(v), .groups = "drop") |>
    arrange(msq)
}
impact_interval <- function(cv, lo, hi) {
  g <- seq(lo, hi, length.out = 200)
  v <- approx(cv$msq, cv$v, xout = g, rule = 2)$y
  c(min(v), max(v))
}
fwb <- bind_rows(lapply(list.files("fwb_msq_coverage",
                                   pattern = "_n[0-9]+[.]rds$", full.names = TRUE),
                        readRDS))
demo <- bind_rows(
  fwb |> filter(cond == "xdim50_k1", item == 11) |> mutate(case = "misfitting, 0 logits"),
  fwb |> filter(cond == "null", item == 11) |> mutate(case = "fitting (null), 0 logits")
)
metrics_demo <- c(C_kl = "KL", F_sem = "F (SEM)", B_shift = "B (SEM)")
bind_rows(lapply(names(metrics_demo), function(m) {
  cv <- curve_for("d20", "on", m)
  demo |>
    rowwise() |>
    mutate(iv = list(impact_interval(cv, lo, hi)),
           true_v = approx(cv$msq, cv$v, xout = pop, rule = 2)$y) |>
    ungroup() |>
    mutate(metric = metrics_demo[[m]], low = vapply(iv, `[`, 1, 1),
           high = vapply(iv, `[`, 1, 2))
})) |>
  group_by(case, metric, n) |>
  summarise(msq_interval = sprintf("%.2f to %.2f", median(lo), median(hi)),
            impact_interval = sprintf("%.3f to %.3f", median(low), median(high)),
            true_impact = sprintf("%.3f", median(true_v)),
            coverage = 100 * mean(true_v >= low - 1e-9 & true_v <= high + 1e-9),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(case, metric, n) |>
  kb(digits = 1)
```

The intervals are medians over the 200 datasets per cell, and coverage is the
share of datasets whose impact interval contains the impact at the item's
population MSQ. Because the mapping is monotone on each side of 1, coverage
follows the coverage of the MSQ interval.

## Relation to Part A

Part A used the d20 design with normal persons and three misfitting items. Its
misfitting items had population MSQ 1.43 (0 logits), 1.37 (-1) and 1.27 (-2)
at $\rho = .15$, 1.27, 1.23 and 1.17 at $\rho = .50$, and 1.14, 1.12 and 1.09 at
$\rho = .75$. With one misfitting item at $\rho = .50$, the item at 0 logits had
1.38. Comparing these with the calibrated $\delta^+$ shows which of them the
floor would flag at each tolerance.

The cascade-affected items in Part A had MSQ about 0.92, which is overfit. Whether
the floor clears them depends on $\delta^-$, the lower side of the band, which
second-dimension misfit cannot calibrate. That check needs an overfit
mechanism (for example a slope above 1) and is not part of this study.

## Interpretation

Written 2026-10-12 after the run. 90 cells (54 at n = 20,000, 36 for the
stability check), 3,600 replicates, none failed, a few minutes on 10 cores. At
$\rho = 1$ every impact metric is exactly 0 and the MSQ is 1.00, as the
counterfactual requires.

**1. The calibration does not depend on n.** For the on-target items, every
metric at n = 2,000 and 5,000 agrees with n = 20,000 within Monte Carlo
noise, at every $\rho$. Because (a) and (b) share all data except item $i$,
estimation noise cancels and does not inflate the absolute or squared
metrics. So the calibration can run at a moderate n.

**2. In a 20-item test, one second-dimension item barely affects accuracy or
individual scores.** Even at $\rho = .3$ (MSQ about 1.5), RMSE against
$\theta_1$ rises by at most 1 percent, the mean score shift is 0.11 to 0.17
SEM, and almost nobody moves by more than 1 SEM. Tolerances on A and B are
not reached within the grid. Metric A is nearly flat for d20, which is why
its rank correlation with MSQ is only 0.6 to 0.7, and it cannot be inverted
there.

**3. The metrics that do respond in a long test are KL, group bias and
conditional bias.** For d20, KL reaches .03 at MSQ 1.29 to 1.39. The
spurious group difference reaches 0.05 SD per SD of the item-specific factor
only for the on-target item, at MSQ 1.41. The worst conditional bias reaches
0.25 SEM at MSQ 1.53 (on target), 1.40 (mid) and 1.26 (off target). KL
responds before the mean shift does, because it squares the shift and is
driven by the persons who move most.

**4. Targeting runs in opposite directions for different metrics.** The
off-target item has the smallest MSQ and the smallest average impact (B, C,
E), but the largest conditional bias (F): its misfit concentrates on the
persons it is targeted at, in the tail. For a scale used against a cut-point
in that tail, the off-target item is the one that matters.

**5. A 9-item polytomous scale is far more sensitive.** For phq9, every
metric reaches its tolerance: RMSE +2.5 percent at MSQ 1.36 to 1.42, mean
shift 0.25 SEM at 1.40 to 1.46, KL .03 at 1.17 to 1.20, group bias 0.05 SD at
1.20 to 1.29, and conditional bias 0.25 SEM at 1.22 to 1.28. The band is
narrower because each item carries more of the score.

**6. The calibrated bands depend on test length and on the tolerance, not
mainly on the item.** Within a design the three items give similar
$\delta^+$ for most metrics (for example KL .03: 0.29 to 0.39 for d20, 0.17 to
0.20 for phq9). Across designs and metrics $\delta^+$ ranges from about 0.17
to more than 0.5. This is the consequence-based version of the Part A
finding that no fixed band works everywhere.

**7. Keeping a misfitting item is usually better than removing it.** In d20
the RMSE with the item kept is 1.5 to 2.5 percent lower than with it
removed at every $\rho$, down to .3. In phq9 keeping is better until MSQ
about 1.5 ($\rho$ about .6). This is more favourable to keeping than the
linear-composite heuristic in the memory notes (crossover near $\rho = .72$
for 20 items), so that heuristic should not be relied on for IRT scoring.

**8. The sum score behaves like the WLE.** With complete data, the rank
correlations with $\theta_1$ are identical, as expected. The group bias in
sum-score SD units is close to the WLE value, slightly smaller in d20.

**9. One misfitting item already causes a cascade.** In phq9 at $\rho = .3$
the other items fall to MSQ 0.87 to 0.89, on the overfit side. Whether the
floor clears them depends on $\delta^-$, from the overfit arm below.

**Overfit arm (added 2026-10-12).** 48 cells, 1,920 replicates, none failed.

**10. A steep item does less harm than an equally large underfit.** A slope
of 3 brings the MSQ down to 0.64 to 0.72 in d20 and about 0.60 in phq9. In
d20 none of the tolerances is reached within the grid (departures up to 0.28
to 0.36), except conditional bias for the off-target item (0.25 SEM at
1 − MSQ = 0.21). In phq9, KL reaches .03 at 0.25 to 0.29, RMSE +2.5 percent at
0.29 to 0.37, and conditional bias 0.25 SEM at 0.19 to 0.28. Compared with the
upper side for phq9 (KL .03 at 0.17 to 0.20), the band is wider below 1 than
above: roughly [0.72, 1.18] for KL .03.

**11. Reported precision stays honest.** The ratio of true error to reported
SEM with the steep item, over the same with a fitting item (metric D), is
0.99 to 1.00 throughout. The claim that overfit makes the SEM or reliability
too optimistic does not hold for a steep slope. It is more likely a property
of redundancy between items (local dependence), which this arm does not
generate.

**12. A steep item costs a little accuracy, and keeping it still beats
removing it.** RMSE rises by up to 2 percent (d20) and 4 percent (phq9) at a
slope of 3, because Rasch scoring gives the item the same weight as the
others when it deserves more. Keeping it is still better than removing it in
every cell except the d20 off-target item at a slope of 3, where the two are
equal.

**13. The cascade from a steep item goes the other way.** One steep item
pushes the other items' MSQ up, to at most 1.04 (d20) and 1.06 (phq9), well
inside any upper band calibrated here.

**Joint arm (added 2026-10-12).** 18 cells, 720 replicates.

**14. Misfitting items do more harm together than separately, and their MSQ
shows less of it.** With three items on a shared second dimension, KL is 1.2
to 1.5 times the sum of the three single-item KLs in d20, and 1.4 to 1.7 times
in phq9. Conditional bias is well above the largest single-item value. Accuracy
(A), flat for single items in d20, rises by up to 12 percent jointly, and by up
to 65 percent in phq9. Group bias (E) is roughly additive. At the same time,
each item's MSQ is *smaller* than when it misfits alone (d20 at $\rho = .3$:
1.39, 1.34 and 1.25 jointly, against 1.54, 1.52 and 1.43 alone), because the
misfitting items now make up part of the total score that defines the
expected responses.

**15. So per-item bands fail when a coherent group of items misfits.** The
joint band on the items' mean MSQ is 0.01 to 0.04 in phq9 for every metric
except the share moving more than 1 SEM
(three of nine items on a second dimension), and 0.02 (KL) to 0.18 in d20.
The impact is large while the MSQ hardly moves. This is not a calibration
problem that a tighter band can fix: a subscale shows up in dimensionality
diagnostics (residual PCA, Martin-Löf, Q3 clusters) better than in item fit.
In the joint condition the reported SEM also becomes too optimistic as a
measure of error in $\theta_1$ (metric D up to 1.21 in d20 and 2.07 in phq9),
because the scores measure a composite.

**16. Removing a coherent misfitting group can pay off.** In d20, keeping the
three items is better than removing them down to $\rho$ about .5. In phq9,
removing them is better below $\rho$ of about .75. At $\rho = .6$ the RMSE is
14 percent higher with the three items kept than with them removed.

**Response dependence arm (added 2026-10-12).** 42 cells, 1,680 replicates.

**17. Response dependence produces overfit in the dependent item, with small
consequences.** At $\lambda = 2$ the dependent item's MSQ falls to 0.86 to
0.87 in d20 and 0.78 to 0.85 in phq9, and the target item's to 0.93 to 0.98.
In d20 no tolerance is reached except RMSE +2.5 percent for the off-target
pair. In phq9 KL reaches .03 at $1 - \text{MSQ}$ = 0.13 to 0.18 and RMSE +2.5
percent at 0.12 to 0.13. Per unit of MSQ departure, response dependence
harms more than a steep slope (phq9 KL .03 at 0.25 to 0.29 for the slope),
so the lower band it implies is narrower, about 0.85 in phq9.

**18. One dependent pair barely changes reported precision.** Metric D is
1.01 to 1.02 in d20 and at most 1.04 in phq9, so the SEM is at most 4 percent
too optimistic. The 5 percent tolerance is not reached. The optimism about
precision that local dependence is known for needs more than one pair, or a
stronger dependence.

**19. MSQ is not monotone in the strength of dependence.** In phq9 the
dependent item's MSQ is lowest at $\lambda$ around 1 to 1.5 and rises again
at 2, while KL and the score shift keep growing. The inversion along the grid
reads the first crossing, which is right for moderate dependence, but MSQ is
a poor guide to strong dependence. Q3 or the log-linear dependence parameter
itself would be.

**Impact intervals.**

**20. The mapping works and reads naturally.** For the misfitting item at 0
logits ($\rho = .50$, normal persons), the median interval at n = 2,000 is a
KL of .032 to .041, a mean score shift of 0.12 to 0.15 SEM, and a worst
conditional bias of 0.13 to 0.20 SEM, around the true values .036, 0.135 and
0.160. For a fitting item the intervals start at 0 and end at .011 (KL),
0.04 (B) and 0.03 (F) at n = 2,000. Coverage is 90.5 to 96.5 percent,
inherited from the MSQ interval, since the mapping is monotone on each side
of 1. This coverage does not test the impact curve itself, which was
calibrated on resampled WLE persons while the FWB data used normal persons.

**Relation to Part A.** With KL .03 as the tolerance, the d20 bands are about
1.29 (0 logits), 1.31 (-1) and 1.39 (-2) on the upper side, and wider than
0.28 to 0.36 below 1 (the tolerance is not reached within the grid). Part A's
misfitting items at $\rho = .15$ (1.43, 1.37, 1.27) would be flagged at 0 and
-1 logits but not at -2, and its items at $\rho = .50$ and .75 would not be
flagged at all. Its cascade-affected items, at MSQ about 0.92, lie far inside
the lower band and would be cleared at any n large enough to make the
interval narrow. So with impact-calibrated bands the cascade does not lead to
flags. The calibration treats one misfitting item at a time, while Part A had
three. Several misfitting items together have a larger joint impact than
each alone, so per-item bands are too lenient when several items misfit. A
joint calibration, or recalibration after the worst item is dealt with, is
needed for that case.

**Limits.** Four mechanisms (second dimension, steep slope, three items on a
shared second dimension, and response dependence between one pair), two
designs, and resampled WLE persons with a discrete distribution. The joint
and dependence arms use one configuration each (three items, one pair). The
tolerances are illustrations.
